documents.title: NHMRC clinical practice guidelines for depression

chunks.content: Introduction Depression and anxiety are prevalent psychiatric disorders that are associated with high rates of disability and suicide, which have been increasingly becoming a major challenge to global public health [ – ]. According to the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study [ , ], approximately 341 million people worldwide suffer from depression, and about 53.9 million are troubled by anxiety disorders. Despite the availability of evidence-based prevention and treatment interventions, these psychiatric disorder continue to impose great mental stress and heavy economic burdens to patients, and also give rise to numerous social problems. It is noteworthy that comorbidity of anxiety and depression reached as high as 50% to 60% [ ]. This comorbidity is associated with a substantially increased risk of suicidal ideation (SID) and suicide attempts, which provide substantial challenges for clinical diagnosis and treatment decisions [ – ]. Therefore, the precise discrimination of depression, anxiety and their comorbidities, along hierarchical management, has received increasing attention and become a research hotspot in the current field of mental health. Currently, the diagnosis of psychiatric disorders primarily relies on clinical interviews and clinician-administered scales. However, these methods are limited by subjective assessment, clinician-patient communication, and cultural influences, which may lead to diagnostic bias or misdiagnosis [ , ]. Given the substantial overlap in clinical symptoms and the potentially shared neurobiological mechanisms among anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity, traditional symptom-based diagnostic approaches often lack sufficient specificity for differential identification [ – ]. However, studies in the past have shown depression or anxiety as distinct disorders, whereas relatively few have specifically focused on the differential diagnosis for comorbid of anxiety and depression [ , ]. In addition, some studies rely on complex or less accessible features, and many lack sufficient interpretability or clinically oriented evaluation, which may limit their application in routine clinical practice. Therefore, there is an urgent requirement to develop cost-effective and accurate auxiliary diagnostic tools to improve the identification and risk stratification of anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity. Heart rate variability (HRV) is a non-invasive indicator used to evaluate autonomic nervous system (ANS) function, which objectively reflects the dynamic balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity [ , ]. Previous studies have consistently demonstrated that patients with depression or anxiety exhibit significantly lower HRV, which reflect diminished ability to regulate emotions and physiological responses to stress [ , ]. These findings indicated that HRV is expected to become an important potential biomarker for clinical diagnosis, disease stratification and prognosis assessment of psychiatric disorders [ – ]. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data sciences, machine learning (ML) has become widely used in public health and medical research fields [ – ]. In recent years, ML-based models have demonstrated outstanding performance in the early diagnosis and screening of psychiatric disorders such as depression or anxiety, particularly in evaluating treatment response and prognosis [ , ]. Thus, we hypothesize that incorporating HRV features and clinical indicators may yield promising efficiency in distinguishing early-stage depression, anxiety, and psychiatric comorbidities. In this study, we aimed to develop and validate an interpretable, multi-task ML prediction model for the early and accurate discrimination of depression alone, anxiety alone, and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. By analyzing the relationship between HRV feature and psychiatric symptoms, we explored how these variables might affect psychiatric disorders. The SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) method was used to visualize feature contributions and enhance the interpretability of models, which is helpful for providing clinical decision-making for clinicians. Methods Study design The study design adheres to the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement. The overall workflow of this study is illustrated in Fig. , which comprises three main components: data acquisition, feature extraction, model construction and validation. Study population This retrospective study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University (KY2024507), with the requirement for informed consent waived. All patient-related information was anonymous and de-identified. The study protocol was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Data of patients who underwent psychological assessment between March 2024 and April 2025, were obtained from the Department of Psychiatry, the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) aged ≥ 14 years; (ii) cognitive ability to understand and complete assessments of the depression and anxiety scale, including HRV measurements; (iii) no gender restrictions; (iv) no severe major cardiovascular diseases, liver or kidney dysfunction. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) patients with missing HRV data; (ii) presence of other psychiatric disorders, such as bipolar disorder or personality disorders; (iii) patients with severe cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart failure or coronary artery disease), chronic liver or kidney disease, or other diseases potentially affecting HRV (e.g., acute infection or fever); and

Southwest Medical University. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) aged ≥ 14 years; (ii) cognitive ability to understand and complete assessments of the depression and anxiety scale, including HRV measurements; (iii) no gender restrictions; (iv) no severe major cardiovascular diseases, liver or kidney dysfunction. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) patients with missing HRV data; (ii) presence of other psychiatric disorders, such as bipolar disorder or personality disorders; (iii) patients with severe cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart failure or coronary artery disease), chronic liver or kidney disease, or other diseases potentially affecting HRV (e.g., acute infection or fever); and (iv) pregnant or breastfeeding women. In this study, a total of 546 patients were included, 114 patients with anxiety, 100 patients with depression, and 332 patients with comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The task of discriminating psychiatric comorbidities was recast into two binary classification events: (i) anxiety versus (vs.) comorbidity of anxiety and depression, and (ii) depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression. According to different tasks, patients were respectively divided into training and validation sets at an approximately 7:3 ratio. Stratified random sampling was employed to ensure that the proportion of positive and negative samples was consistent in the two sets. The flowchart of the study population in Fig. . Clinical assessment and HRV measurement The clinical diagnosis and HRV measurements of patients in the study were rigorously performed by trained psychiatrists in accordance with standardized procedures to ensure consistency and accuracy. According to patient self-reports and clinical interviews, we employed clinician-administered scales to assess various dimensions of psychiatric symptoms, including mood, somatic discomfort, and cognitive function. Outcome measures for diagnosing anxiety, depression and comorbidities assessed included the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24) [ , ] and the 14-item Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA-14) [ , ]. The HAMD-24 was used to evaluate the level of depressive symptoms. The total score of HAMD Scale < 8 is no depression, 8–19 is mild depression, 20–34 is moderate depression, and ≥ 35 is severe depression. The HAMA-14 was used to evaluate the severity of anxious symptoms. The total score of HAMA Scale < 7 is no anxiety, 7–13 is possible anxiety, 14–20 is moderate anxiety, and ≥ 21 is severe anxiety. To reduce potential misclassification due to mild symptom presentation or subjective bias, the comorbidity of anxiety and depression was included when participants met at least moderate symptom severity based on Hamilton scale cutoffs (HAMD ≥ 20 and HAMA ≥ 14). The HRV measurements were conducted using a HRV analyzer system (VitalScan, Credit Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Sichuan, China; https://www.creditpharma.com/ ). Participants were instructed to get sufficient sleep and avoid excessive drinking, smoking, taking caffeine or drugs, and strenuous exercise prior to testing. The HRV measurement environment was maintained with quiet, bright, and soft lighting, block out external noise, and keep a suitable room temperature (20–25℃) to reduce external interference. The electrodes were connected to the three-lead electrocardiogram signal at the standard position, and the basic subject’s information is entered on the operation interface. Subsequently, electrocardiogram (ECG) signals were continuously collected within 5 min for HRV analysis. Upon completion, the system automatically generated and stored an individualized HRV report for each participant. Data collection and preprocessing A total of 17 features were screened out from the case reports, including 2 demographic features (gender, age), 2 clinical features (BMI, heart rate), and 13 HRV features. The HRV features include time-domain features, frequency-domain features, and nonlinear features, which are details in Table . After splitting the training and the validation set, the synthetic minority over-sampling algorithm (SMOTE) was used to balance the positive and negative samples in the training set [ ]. Then, we utilized the Yeo-Johnson power transformation for data normalization. The transformation parameters were fitted in the training set and subsequently applied to the validation set to ensure the model consistency and avoid data leakage [ ]. To prevent over-fitting and increased the generalization ability of the model, the recursive feature elimination (RFE) algorithm with 10-fold cross-validation was used for feature selection [ ]. This method iteratively eliminates features in a backward manner, ranking feature importance and retaining the subset with the strongest discriminative ability [ ]. Through 10-fold cross-validation, the number of retained features (k) is determined in the training set, and then we selected the top k ranked important features to construct models for each task. Model development and validation Six machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and Naïve Bayes (NB) were adopted to develop prediction models for discriminating psychiatric comorbidities, respectively (Supplementary Appendix S1).Then, a comparison of these models was also performed in both the training and validation set. To ensure the stability and generalization ability of the models, a grid search combined with 10-fold

of retained features (k) is determined in the training set, and then we selected the top k ranked important features to construct models for each task. Model development and validation Six machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and Naïve Bayes (NB) were adopted to develop prediction models for discriminating psychiatric comorbidities, respectively (Supplementary Appendix S1).Then, a comparison of these models was also performed in both the training and validation set. To ensure the stability and generalization ability of the models, a grid search combined with 10-fold cross validation was used to determine the best hyperparameters [ , ] (Supplementary Appendix , Table a and b). The discrimination ability of these models was evaluated using multiple metrics, including the area of receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC), accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SEN), specificity (SPE), positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). The 1,000-bootstrap resamples strategy was used for internal validation, and the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was calculated. The model calibration was evaluated using the Calibration curves accompanied by the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (HL test). Decision curve analysis (DCA) was performed to quantify the net clinical benefit across a range of threshold probabilities, thereby evaluating the potential clinical utility of the predictive models. Model interpretability with Shapley Additive explanation (SHAP) In this study, we utilized SHAP method to quantify the contribution and influence of each feature toward the overall prediction result, thereby providing a visual interpretation for the machine-learning model with the best predictive performance to facilitate clinical decision-making [ , ]. The SHAP value indicates that each feature has a positive or negative impact on the probability of the outcome prediction. Besides, we generated force plots to visualize the key features that affect the decision-making process of the best model. Statistical analysis All statistical analysis were performed using R software (version 4.3.0) and Python (version 3.11.7). Continuous variables were expressed as medians, first (Q1) and third (Q3) quartiles, and ranges, and categorical variables were expressed in terms of frequencies and percentages (%). Comparisons between groups were calculated using the Chi-square or the Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, and the Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test for continuous variables. All P were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics A total of 546 patients, 114 patients in anxiety group(20.88%), 100 patients in depression group (18.32%), and 332 patients in comorbidity of anxiety and depression (60.81%), were included in this study. The baseline characteristics of all patients are shown in Table . The significant group differences were observed in age, gender, heart rate, pNN50, RMSSD, SDSD, VLF, HF, SD1, and SD1/SD2 ( P < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were found for BMI, SDNN, SDNN5, SD2, LF, TP and LF/HF ( P > 0.05). Among the three groups, the proportion of female patients in the comorbidity group (81.63%) was higher than in the anxiety group (70.18%) and the depression group (72.00%). Variable selection We used the RFE algorithm with 10-fold cross-validation to rank the importance of features in the training set for different tasks, and the scoring results for each variable were displayed in a bar plot. For the anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression task, the top 11 feature were selected as independent factors for modelling, such as gender, age, HF, VLF, LF/HF, BMI, heart rate, SDNN5, LF, pNN50, and SD1/SD2 (Supplementary Fig. a). Similarly, for the depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, we ultimately selected the top 11 feature as prediction factors for modelling, including LF, gender, SD2, VLF, SDNN, LF/HF, heart rate, TP, HF, SD1/SD2, and BMI (Supplementary Fig. b). Development and validation of prediction models The performance of six machine-learning models for discriminating psychiatric comorbidities was comprehensively evaluated using AUC, ACC, SEN, SPE, PPV, NPV, F1-score, and MCC. Across two binary classification tasks in this study, the XGBoost model demonstrated superior performance compared with the other five machine-learning models as shown in Fig. . For the task of discriminating the anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, the XGBoost model yielded the AUC of 0.8341 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.761–0.907), F1-score of 0.764 and accuracy of 0.7650 (95% CI:0.682–0.848) in the validation set. (Fig. A and B; Table ). For the task of discriminating the depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, the XGBoost model achieved the AUC of 0.8458 (95% CI:0.775–0.917) F1-score of 0.784 and accuracy of 0.7850 (95% CI:0.704–0.866) in the validation set. (Fig. C and D; Table ). To assess the agreement between the predicted and observed outcomes, we constructed calibration curves (1000 bootstrap resamples) for the XGBoost models across two classification tasks. The calibration plots for all classification tasks remained ideal, indicating good stability and clinical utility of the

and accuracy of 0.7650 (95% CI:0.682–0.848) in the validation set. (Fig. A and B; Table ). For the task of discriminating the depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, the XGBoost model achieved the AUC of 0.8458 (95% CI:0.775–0.917) F1-score of 0.784 and accuracy of 0.7850 (95% CI:0.704–0.866) in the validation set. (Fig. C and D; Table ). To assess the agreement between the predicted and observed outcomes, we constructed calibration curves (1000 bootstrap resamples) for the XGBoost models across two classification tasks. The calibration plots for all classification tasks remained ideal, indicating good stability and clinical utility of the XGBoost model in both the training and validation sets (Fig. ). In addition, we performed decision curve analysis (DCA) to evaluate the potential clinical utility of the models by quantifying the net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. The x-axis represents the threshold probability (ranging from 0 to 1), while the y-axis represents the net clinical benefit at each threshold (Fig. ). Across all classification tasks, the XGBoost model consistently achieved a higher net benefit over a wide range of thresholds, indicating the model’s practical utility in clinical diagnosis and decision-making. Model interpretation and visualisation using the SHAP method In this study, the SHAP method was used to visually interpret the best model (XGBoost). We employed the SHAP values to quantitatively illustrate how each feature affects the final prediction outcomes under different feature combinations. The bar chart shows that the higher SHAP value of feature, where a larger value has a greater influence the model’s prediction. The beeswarm plot SHAP values are colour-coded to reveal the relationship between each features and the prediction outcomes, where blue represents lower feature values and red represents higher feature values. The SHAP force plots provide a visual representation of how each feature influences the final prediction f (x) starting from the model’s baseline prediction value (baseline). For the classification of anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, Fig. A and B shows that gender and age were the most important features that have impact on the prediction outcomes, followed by VLF, pNN50, LF/HF, HF, BMI, SD1/SD2, LF, heart rate, and SDNN5. Among all HRV features, VLF has the highest SHAP influence, indicating that higher VLF levels have a stronger impact on the model’s predictions. Figure C and D correspond to the same individual (comorbidity of anxiety and depression). The HF, pNN50, BMI, SD1/SD2, VLF, and gender are the main risk-increasing indicators for comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Meanwhile, LF and LF/HF are the risk-reducing indicators for this comorbidity, though their contributions are relatively small. The final prediction value is 0.702 (> 0.5), which indicates that this patient has a relatively high risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression. For the classification of depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, Fig. A and B shows that LF and gender were the most important features that have impact on the prediction outcomes, followed by VLF, SD1/SD2, heart rate, HF, BMI, TP, LF/HF, SDNN, and SD2. Among all HRV features, LF has the highest SHAP influence, indicating that higher LF levels have a stronger impact on the model’s predictions. Figure C and D correspond to the another individual (depression). The SD2, BMI, and LF are main risk-increasing factors for comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Meanwhile, gender, SD1/SD2, and heart rate are a risk-reducing factor for this comorbidity, though their contributions are relatively small. The final prediction value reaches 0.318 (< 0.5), which indicates that this patient has a relatively low risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Discussion To our knowledge, machine learning has significant advantages for risk prediction and pattern recognition in complex disorders. This study is the first to develop and evaluate multi-task prediction models to discriminate psychiatric comorbidity status using the HRV features. By comparing six ML algorithms, we identified the the best-performing ML algorithm for predicting risk associated with psychiatric disorders. Across two binary classification tasks, our models demonstrated consistently excellent performance in the validation set, with AUCs (95% CIs) of 0.8341 (95% CI:0.761–0.907) for anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, 0.8458 (95% CI:0.775–0.917) for depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The final model incorporated basic clinical data and HRV features to ensure simplicity, user-friendliness, and potential clinical utility, and also demonstrated strong generalization ability and stability. To improve interpretability and clinical application of models, we employed SHAP to visualized global and local model explanations, which is helpful for providing timely appropriate intervention for patients with psychiatric disorders. Depression, anxiety, and their comorbidity are multifactorial and potentially life-threatening psychiatric disorders, they have similar clinical symptoms and are difficult to strictly discriminate. Our findings showed that anxiety, depression, and comorbidities of anxiety and depression are all significantly associated with reduced HRV features. The demographic features (gender, age) may be associated

To improve interpretability and clinical application of models, we employed SHAP to visualized global and local model explanations, which is helpful for providing timely appropriate intervention for patients with psychiatric disorders. Depression, anxiety, and their comorbidity are multifactorial and potentially life-threatening psychiatric disorders, they have similar clinical symptoms and are difficult to strictly discriminate. Our findings showed that anxiety, depression, and comorbidities of anxiety and depression are all significantly associated with reduced HRV features. The demographic features (gender, age) may be associated with the risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression, potentially linked to differences in hormonal regulation, cognitive development, and emotional processing mechanisms [ , ]. Specifically, comorbid patients exhibit higher resting heart rates and lower HRV characteristic variables (such as RMSSD, SDSD, SD1, SD1/SD2, VLF and HF), which indicated they were significantly autonomic dysregulation compared to patients with depression or anxiety alone. These findings are consistent with previous studies [ – ], which characterized by dual abnormalities of increased sympathetic activity and vagal inhibition, which is specifically characterized by a dual disturbance pattern involving abnormally heightened sympathetic nerve activity and impaired vagal regulatory function. This imbalance affects cardiac autonomic regulation and cause physiological dysfunction across multiple systems through the neuro-humoral regulatory pathway, including the endocrine and digestive systems [ – ]. To further explore the decision-making logic driving model prediction, SHAP analysis were applied to hierarchically interpret the optimal model by providing the feature contributions from the population to the individual level. Compared with traditional feature ranking methods, SHAP can reveal how the model integrates feature information at different levels, thereby significantly enhancing model transparency and clinical interpretability [ ]. For the classification task of anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, SHAP visualizations indicated that VLF, pNN50, LF/HF, and HF were key contributors to the model’s predictions. The decreased VLF has been typically associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk, impaired autonomic nerve function and chronic stress, which may be the reason for more severe autonomic dysfunction observed in comorbid patients [ , ]. The pNN50 mainly reflects the regulatory ability of the parasympathetic nerve relative to heart rate [ ]. The decreased HF leads to vagal dysfunction, exacerbate emotional instability and abnormal stress responses, which may indicate that anxious patients with decreased HF have a potential risk of deteriorating into complex comorbid patients [ ]. Our findings reveal that the elevated LF/HF ratio was positively correlated with comorbidity risk [ ], which may reflect a significant alteration in the autonomic nerve regulation pattern of comorbid patients compared to anxiety patients alone [ ]. For the classification task of depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, SHAP visualizations indicated that LF, VLF, SD1/SD2, heart rate, and HF emerged as the most influential features. The LF primarily reflects the integrated sympathetic-vagal regulatory activity under pressure reflex modulation, the abnormal variation of LF value indicate that comorbid patients may exhibit autonomic dysfunction [ ]. The SD1/SD2 ratio reflects the complexity of autonomic nerve regulation and dynamic adaptability. The decreased SD1/SD2 may reduce the coordinated regulatory ability of the autonomic nervous system, which is consistent with the occurrence of more severe autonomic dysfunction in patients with comorbid anxiety and depression [ ]. The SHAP contributions of LF, VLF, and HF exhibit pronounced nonlinearity across individuals, indicating that they possess heterogeneity rather than simple unidirectional effects when discriminating comorbid patients and depression alone. Our findings reveal that the VLF was correlated with comorbid patients, which indicated that comorbid patients exhibit more complex ANS dysregulation compared to depression or anxiety alone. Notably, VLF proved significant across two classification tasks, highlighting the cross-task value of the autonomic nerve function regulatory mechanisms for identifying complex psychiatric symptom. This finding indicates that VLF may serve as a potential key HRV indicator for identifying comorbidity of anxiety and depression, though the mechanism requires further validation in prospective studies. From a clinical perspective, our findings have potential significant implications for improving symptom management and intervention strategies. HRV, as a non-invasive, accessible, and cost-effective physiological indicator, can rapidly reflect ANS function, which has been widely proved to be closely associated with anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity [ , ]. Therefore, the ML-based models incorporating HRV features can provide clinicians with an objective auxiliary assessment tool for early identification of high-risk individuals. This approach may be particularly valuable in primary care settings or regions with limited healthcare resources, where it can serve as a screening tool to improve the efficiency of identifying suspected patients. Additionally, for patients who have already been diagnosed with anxiety or depression, regular monitoring of HRV indicators can help track disease progression, promptly identify high-risk individuals evolving to comorbidities, and thereby provide targeted interventions strategies. Therefore, the ML-based models incorporating HRV features can provide clinicians with an objective auxiliary assessment tool for early identification of high-risk individuals. This approach may be particularly valuable in primary care settings or regions with limited healthcare resources, where it can serve as a screening tool to improve the efficiency of identifying suspected patients. Additionally, for patients who have already been diagnosed with anxiety or depression, regular monitoring of HRV indicators can help track disease progression, promptly identify high-risk individuals evolving to comorbidities, and thereby provide targeted interventions strategies. However, there were several limitations in our study. Firstly, this retrospective single-center study has a relatively limited-size sample and predominantly adolescent participants (median age 16 years), which may introduce potential selection bias and constrains generalisability to other populations. To address this, future multi-center studies will incorporate prospective data and expand the sample size of different age populations before actual clinical application. Secondly, our findings only included HRV and conventional clinical features, more clinical features such as clinical drug use, follow-up, genes, neuroimaging and inflammatory markers were not included in this study. Thirdly, this study only discriminate psychiatric comorbidity and failed to involve the prediction of treatment responses, thereby preventing the model from accounting for regimen-specific effects. Finally, although HRV serves as a non-invasive indicator of autonomic activity, which represents only an indirect marker of the complex heart-brain interactions for emotional regulation and psychiatric symptoms. In future, we will employ a multimodal approach integrating HRV and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals to conduct comprehensive analyses of individual mental health states. Despite these limitations, our findings provide effective biomarkers for distinguishing individuals with psychiatric disorders, offering valuable support for advancing early prevention and timely intervention. Conclusions This study reveals the relationship between HRV features and different psychiatric symptoms, and explores HRV as a potential biomarker for the diagnosis of anxiety, depression, and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. we developed and validated an interpretable multi-task ML prediction model using HRV for the early and accurate discrimination of depression alone, anxiety alone and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The superior performance highlighted the potential to aid clinical decision-making for the individualized treatment. documents.title: NHMRC Australian clinical practice guideline for borderline personality disorder

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The potentially serious effects of bipolar disorder (BD) on health and wellbeing are well‐recognized: beyond the direct experience of mood symptoms, many individuals with BD experience difficulties with interpersonal relationships [ ], physical health [ ], cognition [ ], and occupational functioning [ ]. Distressing psychological impacts include stigma, disruption to sense of self, and loss of hope [ ]. Optimal treatment of BD therefore involves not only symptom management but also attention to quality of life (QoL), a construct that encompasses health, functioning, well‐being, and satisfaction with various life domains [ , ]. People with BD consider QoL improvements to be as important as symptom reduction when evaluating treatments [ ]. As correlations between mood stability and QoL are typically small to moderate [ ], interventions specifically targeting QoL are warranted. Positively, research demonstrates that individuals with BD can live well by employing various strategies to manage symptoms and improve QoL [ , ]. Self‐management is now recognized as a central component of BD care in major treatment guidelines [ , ]. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), particularly smartphone apps, are one means of improving access to and reach of BD‐related self‐management information and support [ ], and have potential advantages over in‐person care. For example, DMHIs are accessible at a time and place convenient to the user, can be used discreetly, and can provide in‐the‐moment interventions and feedback. However, there is widespread concern about the quality, safety, and efficacy of commercial apps [ ]. A review of publicly available apps for BD found that one third lacked privacy policies, only one was evidence‐based, and several included harmful, stigmatizing, or misleading content [ ]. Individuals with BD report using apps designed for the general public or unipolar depression for mood and sleep self‐management [ ]. This is potentially problematic, as such apps may suggest self‐management strategies that risk triggering or exacerbating manic symptoms [ ]. In a recent review of app‐based interventions for BD, Anmella and colleagues identified 13 evaluations (randomized control trials, RCTs, and observational studies) of 8 interventions [ ]. Most interventions offered self‐monitoring, cognitive behavior therapy, or psychoeducation, alone or in combination. While these strategies fall under the umbrella of self‐management, they may not address broader aspects of QoL and functioning, which people with BD have described as a limitation of current symptom‐focused care [ ]. Two apps identified in the review targeted self‐management skills and addressed aspects of wellness beyond symptoms; however one was designed for serious mental illnesses and not BD specifically. The other app, Life Goals, contained information on BD treatment, symptoms, and lifestyle factors. However, user satisfaction with this app was low, with less than half of the participants endorsing it as helpful in managing their health or supporting wellness goals. To address limitations in the availability of apps targeting the needs and preferences of people with BD, a new DMHI, the PolarUs app, was co‐designed by researchers, healthcare providers, and people with lived experience of BD to support QoL self‐monitoring and self‐management. Core to the app is the Quality of Life in Bipolar Disorder (QoL.BD), a valid and reliable BD‐specific QoL scale [ , ]: app users self‐monitor their QoL using this scale, and the PolarUs content is specifically designed to address QoL.BD‐relevant life domains measured by this scale. The self‐management content of the PolarUs app was drawn in part from an existing website providing evidence‐informed self‐management strategies for BD [ ]. To improve international scalability, the PolarUs app was designed as a fully self‐guided program. In this paper we report on the quantitative outcomes from a mixed methods pilot evaluation of the PolarUs app. Qualitative and behavioral data findings from the study will be reported in subsequent publications. The study had three quantitative objectives: 1. To assess feasibility of the PolarUs app, with feasibility understood as adherence with the app, measured by number of weekly Brief QoL.BD's completed during the intervention period; 2. To test the hypothesis that QoL (measured using the Brief QoL.BD) would improve across the intervention period. Secondary efficacy outcomes included mood symptoms, self‐efficacy in illness management, subjective recovery, and self‐compassion; 3. To investigate the association between adherence with the PolarUs app and primary and secondary outcomes. Patterns of adherence were assessed using a novel cluster analysis, which was then used as a predictor of primary outcomes. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design Overview and Co‐Design Methods This study was a non‐randomized pilot evaluation of the alpha version of a new app (PolarUs) developed to support QoL self‐monitoring and self‐management in people with BD [ ]. The target sample size was 150 adults with a confirmed diagnosis of BD residing in North America. The app evaluation period was 12 weeks. A mixed methods research approach [ ], was embedded in the study design; qualitative interviews were

secondary outcomes. Patterns of adherence were assessed using a novel cluster analysis, which was then used as a predictor of primary outcomes. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design Overview and Co‐Design Methods This study was a non‐randomized pilot evaluation of the alpha version of a new app (PolarUs) developed to support QoL self‐monitoring and self‐management in people with BD [ ]. The target sample size was 150 adults with a confirmed diagnosis of BD residing in North America. The app evaluation period was 12 weeks. A mixed methods research approach [ ], was embedded in the study design; qualitative interviews were conducted with a subsample of participants purposefully selected on the basis of quantitatively assessed varied engagement patterns. These data will be reported elsewhere. The PolarUs app was developed using co‐design methods by the Collaborative Research Team to Study Psychosocial Issues in Bipolar Disorder (CREST.BD), which specializes in the inclusion of people with BD in the cycle of research and knowledge exchange [ ]. Lived experiences of BD were fully integrated into both the development of the app and the design and execution of the evaluation study. For example, some study co‐investigators and staff live with BD. App development and study design and delivery were guided over a two‐year period by a 7‐member advisory group. All advisory group members had lived experience of BD and additional expertise such as user interface design, graphic design, and plain language writing. Development of features and content for the app was also informed by the results of a large ( n = 919) international survey of use of and attitudes toward apps among people with BD [ ] and a survey of healthcare providers [ ]. 2.2 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PolarUs</styled-content> App At the heart of the PolarUs app is the QoL.BD scale, which provides both the organizing framework for the app and serves as the primary assessment tool for evaluating QoL outcomes. The QoL.BD is a valid and reliable BD‐specific QoL scale, available in both Full (56‐item) and Brief (12‐item) form [ ]. As described below, the Full QoL.BD assesses wellbeing across 14 QoL domains. The PolarUs app also incorporates the evidence, resources, and tools provided in CREST.BD's Bipolar Wellness Centre [ ], wherein BD self‐management content is organized by 17 areas (recognizing that the QoL.BD physical health domain encompasses diet, exercise, substance use and sexual health); app content is also organized according to these 17 areas. The PolarUs app content, however, represents a major expansion beyond that provided in the Bipolar Wellness Centre. Nested within the 17 QoL areas are 99 concrete self‐management strategies and 350 associated resources to support users with implementing these strategies (e.g., worksheets, videos, webinars, articles), produced by CREST.BD or curated from international evidence‐informed sources. A bank of 1479 discrete daily affirmations were also incorporated in the app. 2.2.1 User Flow In‐app onboarding includes viewing of brief videos explaining the purpose and design of the app and a description of QoL and self‐management in BD. Users are instructed to complete the full QoL.BD at baseline and are provided with feedback on scores across QoL domains. They are then able to select up to three QoL domains to focus on, after which they can select up to four relevant self‐management strategies to implement over the coming month. Once users have selected their self‐management strategies, they are provided with a list of resources related to each strategy to review at their leisure. Users are prompted to complete the Brief QoL.BD on a weekly basis. After 1 month of app use, users are instructed to complete the Full QoL.BD again, at which point they can continue to focus on the same QoL areas or select alternative domains (and strategies) to focus on. The app also incorporates a function for daily monitoring of mood and sleep. Examples of user flow through the app are provided in (Figures , , ). Fulsome description of design features of the PolarUs app are provided elsewhere [ ]. 2.2.2 Technical Specifications The alpha version of the PolarUs app operated on the iOS smartphone platform. Recruitment of the target sample of n = 150 participants was reached in 5 months. Examination of the demographics of this initial sample indicated sub‐optimal diversity; purposeful sampling was therefore used to recruit an additional n = 20 participants prioritizing inclusion of people who identified as trans or non‐binary, or being from diverse ethnocultural backgrounds. Community partners such as the Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA) supported this targeted recruitment by highlighting the study to DBSA peer support group facilitators for Black individuals with mood disorders. For inclusion, participants were required to be residents of North America, aged > 18 years, with a primary DSM Fourth Edition, Text Revision [ ], diagnosis of BD type 1, BD type 2, or BD not otherwise specified as assessed by the Mini‐International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI) version 7.0 [ ]. Minimally restrictive exclusion criteria were set to aid generalizability; those currently experiencing psychosis or with active suicidal ideation as assessed by diagnostic interview were excluded and provided with resource lists. Participants were also required to be iOS smartphone users, agree to install the app, agree to receive app notifications, and have sufficient understanding of written and spoken English to provide informed consent and engage with the app. Ethics approval was obtained from the University of British Columbia Behavioral Research Ethics Board office (H21‐02042). 2.4 Data Collection and Assessment Scales The MINI was administered by research assistants at baseline via Zoom to confirm diagnostic eligibility. This structured baseline interview was also used to record sociodemographic variables and assess exclusion criteria. Clinician‐rated and self‐report scales were completed at baseline and at monthly intervals during the 12‐week study period. All self‐report scales were administered via a secure, encrypted web‐based survey platform (UBC Qualtrics) with data stored on Canadian servers. All data collected by the PolarUs app was transmitted using end‐to‐end encryption to a secure database on a Canadian server. Research assistants monitored the completion of Qualtrics questionnaires on a regular basis and prompted participants to facilitate completion of the online forms when support was required. At the end of the intervention period, a subset of consenting participants was purposefully selected for invitation to participate in qualitative interviews (data not included in this report). Assessment procedures and study instruments are described below and in (Table ). 2.4.1 Brief <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">QoL</styled-content>.<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">BD</styled-content>: Primary Outcome Measure The QoL.BD is the first and (to‐date) only instrument developed to specifically assess QoL in terms of the life areas prioritized by people with BD [ ]. The Full 56‐item QoL.BD assesses 12 core (physical, sleep, mood, cognition, leisure, social, spirituality, finance, household, self‐esteem, independence, and identity) and 2 optional (work and study) life areas, each containing 4 self‐report Likert scale items (1: strongly disagree to 5: strongly agree). An overall score (range 48–240) can be calculated by summing the responses to the 48 items of the 12 core domains, with higher scores representing greater life satisfaction. The Brief QoL.BD contains 12 items representing the core domains (overall score range 12–60). During initial field testing, both versions of the QoL.BD had excellent internal reliability (Cronbach α > 0.8), and the Brief QoL.BD demonstrated a higher sensitivity to changes in clinician‐rated symptoms of depression than generic QoL measures [ ]. The QoL.BD has been used in international clinical trials, with sensitivity to treatment effects demonstrated [ ]. Construct validity of the Brief and full QoL.BD has been demonstrated through associations with symptoms of mania and depression, generic QoL instruments, and functioning [ , ]. A web‐based adaptation of the full instrument, the QoL Tool, has been psychometrically validated [ ]. The Brief QoL.BD served as the primary outcome measure in this study; study feasibility was operationalized as the number of in‐app weekly completions of the Brief QoL.BD. 2.4.2 Mood Rating Scales The 10‐item Montgomery‐Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) [ ], was administered using a structured interview guide [ ]; MADRS scores range from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating greater severity of depressive symptoms. Symptoms of mania were assessed using the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) [ ], an 11‐item scale with scores ranging from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating greater severity of manic symptoms. 2.4.3 Self‐Report Scales The Brief World Health Organization Quality of Life

Chronic Disease Self‐Efficacy was assessed using the 5‐item Manage Disease in General subscale of Stanford's Chronic Disease Self‐Efficacy Scale (SEMDG) [ ]. Self‐reported mood was measured using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) [ ]. The 36‐item Bipolar Recovery Questionnaire was used to measure experiences of personal (versus clinical) recovery in BD [ ]. Demographic questions assessed sex and gender and included the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status [ ]. 2.4.4 Sample Size To inform sample size, we benchmarked a meta‐analysis of clinical trials of smartphone apps for depressive symptoms, which estimated dropout rates of 25% to 50% [ ]. Allowing for a 33% dropout rate, 90% power, an effect size of 0.5 SD, and a nonsphericity correction of 0.7 for QoL.BD scores for each participant, the required sample size for addressing Objective 2 (assessing the impact of the PolarUs app on QoL outcomes) was estimated at 150 participants. This sample size also allowed similar power levels to address secondary outcomes. 2.4.5 Statistical Analyses Only participants who completed all baseline assessments were included in analyses ( n = 170). Descriptive statistics for these 170 participants are presented for demographic data and monthly assessments missed (Table ). Scales were computed for the primary and secondary measures with Cronbach's alpha used to assess their reliability. Only in the case of the Bipolar Recovery scale were there missing items for some months; these values were imputed using the Expectation Maximization method, assuming that data were missing completely at random. To assess Objective 1 (to assess feasibility of the PolarUs app, with feasibility understood as adherence with the app, operationalized as number of weekly Brief QoL.BD's completed over the intervention period, rather than more study‐centric feasibility outcomes, such as recruitment or enrollment rates) descriptive statistics were presented on adherence rates overall and across the study period. Potential associations between the number of missed assessments and demographic data were examined using a Generalized Linear Model to predict the number of weekly Brief QoL.BD assessments missed, assuming a Binomial distribution but allowing for over‐dispersion. To assess Objective 2 (to test the hypothesis that QoL would improve across the intervention period), a linear mixed model was fitted to the data for the primary outcome measure (weekly Brief QoL.BD) assuming a random intercept and slope. In this model we controlled for country of residence as a fixed factor. This was an intention‐to‐treat analysis, carried out without and with the multiple imputation (MI) of missing data, both assuming that data was missing at random. In both analyses the model was fitted using the Full Maximum Likelihood approach. A similar analysis was also carried out for the monthly secondary measures after first testing for normality and establishing the nature of the correlation structure for these scales across time, using a random intercept model to estimate the intra‐cluster correlation coefficient (ICC). Finally, marginal means were computed for the monthly assessments with effect sizes (Cohen's d) provided for changes over the intervention period. To assess Objective 3 (to investigate the association between adherence with the PolarUs app and primary and secondary outcomes) a Hierarchical cluster analysis was conducted with the number of Brief QoL.BD assessments completed in the 4‐to‐5‐week periods between clinical assessments (i.e., adherence data) using Ward's method, with the best results obtained for the Silhouette measure when there were four clusters. The clusters were graphically compared in terms of their adherence over time and their mean Brief QoL.BD scores in each 4‐to‐5‐week period. However, cluster 3 (Regularly Used Stable: n = 65) did not show improvement, despite starting from a relatively low base. 4 Discussion This paper described the feasibility and impact of the alpha version of the PolarUs app for BD, as assessed via a single‐arm pilot study. Specific objectives addressed were: (1) To assess feasibility of the PolarUs app, with feasibility understood as adherence with the app, operationalized by completion of weekly in‐app Brief QoL.BD assessments; (2) To test the hypothesis that QoL (measured on the Brief QoL.BD) would improve across the intervention period and to explore secondary efficacy outcomes; and (3) To investigate the association between app adherence and primary and secondary outcomes by way of cluster analysis. With respect to feasibility (adherence) outcomes, as with many mental health apps, we observed a gradual decline in adherence over the study period. With respect to primary and secondary outcomes, positively, significant improvements were observed in our primary outcome of QoL, as well as assessor‐rated symptoms of mania and depression, and self‐compassion. Our cluster analysis of adherence rates provided more granular insights on usage patterns and associated impacts, with four distinct clusters displaying varying relationships between adherence, baseline QoL, and trajectories of QoL improvement. A recent systematic review of adherence rates to smartphone apps in BD suggested activity rates between 58%–91% [ ], while another review of general DHMI's showed high variability across real‐world and research studies [ , ]. This may be because the quality of reporting on adherence is poor and unstandardized; for example, downloading the app versus completing all components of the intervention [ ]. The current study operationalized adherence as completion of the QoL self‐assessments. This has two implications for our interpretation of adherence. First, our estimate of adherence may not directly map onto engagement, as participants could still access psychoeducation materials and resources without completing these assessments. Second, most research studies collect non‐obtrusive behavioral data, e.g., number of logins, pages or app features accessed, time spent [ ], that requires no additional effort on the part of app users. A recent systematic review of DMHIs for BD confirmed that use of mental health apps should be as low‐effort as possible by reducing barriers related to accessing and interacting with the app and its content [ ]; completing the monthly assessment may have increased some participants' cognitive load resulting in lower completion levels, even as they continued to use and potentially benefit from PolarUs. Indeed, qualitative data explored in detail elsewhere highlighted some barriers to completion of QoL self‐assessments, including negative emotional responses to seeing lower than desired responses to self‐monitoring data [ ], and a higher level of perceived effort associated with the longer weekly and monthly QoL self‐assessments as compared to daily check‐in items [ ]. Future evaluations of the PolarUs app will therefore incorporate exploratory analyses of behavioral indicators of engagement collected in‐app. Further, it is difficult to determine the ‘dose’ of DMHIs required for meaningful user impact, and different people may benefit from different ‘doses' [ ]. As a result, usage data may offer only part of the picture when it comes to user engagement with DMHIs, and may not account for subjective relevance or utility. In this study, QoL—not user engagement—was the primary outcome variable, and this differs from many commercial health applications. User engagement in DMHI research is often bluntly equated to behavioral metrics of app usage rather than a holistic interpretation of usage and its relationship to positive health outcomes [ , ]. As noted, QoL is an individualized experience: “individuals with BD locate their QoL in relation to a variety of reference points drawn from past experiences, social context or expectations for the future” [ ]. User engagement in DMHI research is often bluntly equated to behavioral metrics of app usage rather than a holistic interpretation of usage and its relationship to positive health outcomes [ , ]. As noted, QoL is an individualized experience: “individuals with BD locate their QoL in relation to a variety of reference points drawn from past experiences, social context or expectations for the future” [ ]. This study allowed participants to select QoL indicators most relevant to their situation and goals, and to select strategies to work toward these goals. Thus, an area for future analysis of this data will be to determine if there are different patterns of engagement for QoL areas based on the self‐report and usage data we collected. A forthcoming qualitative analysis will also explore in greater detail factors that influenced engagement with the app [ ]. This qualitative data will complement the present quantitative analysis by exploring salient aspects of engagement from the perspective of participants, including both usage of various app features (self‐monitoring and psychoeducational materials), as well as out of app experiences (e.g., cognitive and emotional responses to app content, attempts to enact self‐management strategies). We expect these analyses will generate hypotheses for potential differing patterns of app usage and benefit reported in this study, and will inform the selection of additional data that should be quantitatively collected and explored in future evaluations. Low adherence rates with apps may also stem from a dearth of user involvement in app development processes. A prior review found only two of eleven mental health self‐monitoring apps used in research with people with BD could be classified as having a high level of user involvement, defined as users having input across the full spectrum of app development, from conceptualization, to prototype design, to evaluation [ ]. Of the two apps identified in this aforementioned review that were developed with high user involvement, neither were designed for BD . A significant strength of this study lies in the fact that it was conducted within a Community Based Participatory Research framework involving people with lived experience of BD and co‐design methods integrated into the app development, study design and execution, and knowledge exchange phases. One notable study limitation relates to the generalizability of our findings. Regarding language accessibility, the alpha version of the PolarUs app was only available in English; none of its content was translated nor culturally adapted. Lack of availability of culturally and linguistically appropriate interventions represents a substantial barrier to equitable access to DMHIs [ ], with representatives of ethnocultural and linguistic minorities often not included in the development and testing of DMHIs [ ]. Many DMHIs are therefore not designed to reflect social and cultural diversity, which can lead to low acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness of interventions among these populations [ ]. This is despite the fact that interest in DMHI appears to be high among ethnic and racial minorities [ ], suggesting that failure to provide culturally appropriate interventions undercuts their potential as acceptable treatments in these populations. Further limiting generalizability of our findings is the likelihood that participants with a specific interest in DMHIs and self‐management of BD self‐selected into the research project. Although we aimed to make the PolarUs app as accessible as possible through community consultation, consideration of accessibility issues specific to serious mental health issues during the design phase [ ], and attention to reading level in content writing, it is still likely that individuals with more familiarity with apps and computers will be better able to engage with the intervention and complete all required research tasks (i.e., web‐based questionnaires). Individuals with BD who report using self‐management apps for mood and sleep demonstrate higher levels of digital health literacy [ ]; therefore, individuals with less confidence in navigating DMHIs may have been less likely to take up or adhere to PolarUs. Although it was not feasible for us to offer dedicated supports to upskill participants in technological abilities in the context of this study, future research may evaluate whether adjunctive interventions can enhance the feasibility of DMHIs in populations with BD. Our sample was also highly educated and over half of the sample reported being in full‐time employment. Most importantly in terms of limitations is the non‐controlled nature of our pilot data; a fully powered RCT is required to definitively assess the efficacy of the PolarUs app. Positioning this study within the context of the wider DMHI literature, it is encouraging to see that other DMHIs designed for BD populations are in development and/or evaluation. Most importantly in terms of limitations is the non‐controlled nature of our pilot data; a fully powered RCT is required to definitively assess the efficacy of the PolarUs app. Positioning this study within the context of the wider DMHI literature, it is encouraging to see that other DMHIs designed for BD populations are in development and/or evaluation. Notable is the LiveWell [ ], self‐management app, designed to reduce relapse risk and improve QoL in BD. Outcomes of a recently published RCT ( n = 205) did not detect a difference in the primary outcome of time to relapse, but positive effects were observed for depression symptom severity and relational QoL. The LiveWell app has a number of strengths, including a user‐centered development process and integration of content addressing both symptoms and QoL. Inclusion of human support in the intervention through six one‐to‐one motivational interviewing coaching sessions and data sharing with healthcare providers may support effective engagement. However, these roles are also a barrier to scalability, as implementation of LiveWell as designed will require dedicated coaching staff and resources. Furthermore, the planned integration of the app in clinical care means it may not reach individuals who are not utilizing formal services due to their inaccessibility, issues of stigma, or beliefs about treatment. We look forward to a time when people with BD will have access to a palette of options for evidence‐based DMHIs, allowing for self‐selection of apps according to user preferences, needs and context. The PolarUs app, a DMHI specifically targeting QoL and self‐management in BD designed for scalability (i.e., primarily designed for use as a self‐guided program) may add a valuable option in the DMHI landscape. One perennial problem lies in the fact that research‐led DMHIs are rarely made publicly available [ ]; researchers are increasingly encouraged, therefore, to formulate plans for sustainable dissemination. To accelerate public access to the PolarUs app we secured philanthropic support from the Daymark Foundation in Canada to advance development of the English language version of the PolarUs app for full market release on iOS and Android platforms. In parallel with data collection for the study reported here, we underwent a 2 year co‐design and development period to produce a significantly advanced beta version of the PolarUs app and the content contained within it. App advances include substantial improvements to user experience and user interface design and additional self‐monitoring options and graphical feedback. With attention to accessibility and diversity, a comprehensive refresh of PolarUs content was conducted: key messages, audiovisual alternatives, and effort ratings were added and new resources tailored for diverse communities (e.g., ethnocultural/racialized, older adults, LGBTQ2S+, Indigenous communities). A future avenue of research will be to evaluate real‐world patterns of uptake and engagement with the beta app to better understand the feasibility of PolarUs across diverse naturalistic settings, including resource‐constrained environments. Further supporting our goal of ensuring the PolarUs app is feasible across cultures, funding has been obtained to culturally adapt the PolarUs app for ethnoculturally diverse communities and to definitively test the efficacy of the advanced app in improving QoL in diverse people with BD within an RCT design. The results of the present evaluation of the PolarUs app are encouraging and add to a solid body of literature supporting the potential of self‐management for optimizing health and QoL for people with BD and the relatively nascent literature on the effective DMHIs for the condition. However, not all individuals with BD will be interested in, able to access, or able to use DMHIs. Previous qualitative investigations of how service users with serious mental illnesses viewed DMHIs have flagged concerns that such tools would replace support options delivered by a person [ ]. As such, supporting individuals with BD to access evidence‐based self‐management and support through diverse intervention streams is important. Catering to individuals who prioritize human interaction, we are developing a non‐app form of intervention delivery, leveraging the content and resources within the PolarUs app to create a peer‐delivered group psychoeducation program. Similar to DMHIs, peer support has been identified as a means to improve access to and affordability of mental healthcare [ , , ]. Peer support can offer additional benefits for subjective recovery: qualitative data from a previous CREST.BD intervention evaluation highlighted unique benefits for individuals who participated in a face‐to‐face group workshop, including reduced self‐stigma, increased self‐compassion, and self‐efficacy [ , ]. By developing a variety of scalable and effective app and non‐app self‐management interventions (to be used alone or in combination), we hope to extend the reach of evidence‐based self‐management information to all individuals with BD who would benefit.
